## Simple explanation

Interpretability is the effort to understand why a model behaves as it does.
It can mean examining how a model uses its inputs, which patterns it has
learned, or what factors contributed to a particular prediction.

## Technical explanation

Interpretability methods include inherently inspectable models and
post-hoc analyses of more complex models. Explanations may be local, for a
single prediction, or global, describing behavior across a model or dataset.
Methods include feature attribution, example-based explanations, and
mechanistic analysis of internal representations.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Interpretability can help detect unwanted shortcuts, debug failures, support
review, and form hypotheses about model behavior. It is especially relevant
when model decisions have significant consequences, but explanation quality
and the intended use of an explanation must be evaluated carefully.

## How it works

An analysis starts with a specific question about a model and selects a
method suited to that question. A feature-attribution method, for example,
estimates how input features relate to a prediction. Results should be
checked for stability and against other evidence; an explanation is not
automatically a faithful account of the model's reasoning.

## Practical example

If a classifier labels images of wolves as dogs, an engineer might inspect
saliency maps and compare predictions after changing the background. If the
model relies heavily on snow rather than the animal, that signals a dataset
or modeling problem to investigate.

## Common misconceptions

- An explanation is not necessarily a causal account of a prediction.
- A model that is easy to inspect is not automatically fair, safe, or
  correct.
- One explanation method rarely answers every question about a model.
